Abstract: In this paper, a new communication protocol is proposed to allow direct com-
munication between internet of things (IoT)-enabled home energy management systems
(HEMSs) in a smart microgrid. The direct communication features are an important at-
tribute for decentralised demand management and local energy trading operations in a
microgrid equipped with renewable energy resources. The proposed scheme utilises the in-
termediate HEMSs as relay nodes that forward the sum of the received signals from nearby
HEMSs to both ends of the entire network. The scheme can achieve lower latency compared
to the cases when HEMSs adopt direct decode−and−forward (DF) or transmit through the
central controller. For the proposed protocol, we have analytically obtained expressions
for the error probability at different HEMSs, as well as the average bit error rate (BER) to
indicate the overall error performance of the microgrid communication. To evaluate the
proposed protocol in different channel conditions, numerical simulation is performed. The
results demonstrate that the channel conditions between the HEMSs at the middle of the
network have a greater impact on the system error performance. Overall, it can be observed
that the proposed protocol suffers a lower degradation in error performance in comparison
to direct DF when one of the users experiences worse channel conditions.
Keywords: energy management; decode−and−forward; microgrid; error performance;
wireless communication

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
The unprecedented integration of distributed renewable energy resources (DERs) into
customer premises has led to the evolution of the microgrid. Microgrids have allowed
the utilisation of local energy generation to meet local energy demand with better power
quality resulting from reduced transmission line losses [1–5]. Moreover, microgrids can
enhance the energy security of remotely located communities by reducing dependency
on the main power grid. To enable the reliable operation of a microgrid, effective energy
management systems (EMSs) need to be incorporated so as to control energy sharing within
the microgrid, as well as with the main power grid during contingencies [6]. For effective
energy management operation, it is essential that the power generation and consumption
information in the microgrid is available in real time with reasonable accuracy, hence
arises the need for low-latency and high-reliability communication protocols [ 7–9]. In
essence, this study investigates the design of a new communication scheme that enables
direct communication between HEMSs for the purpose of energy management, where
intermediate HEMSs relay the messages from adjacent HEMSs throughout the network
of HEMSs.

With the advent of information and communication technologies, the concept of
ubiquitous connectivity among every possible device that we use in our day-to-day life has
received significant attention from researchers and the broader community. Such ubiquitous
connectivity among all intelligent devices is often denoted as the internet of things (IoT). A
number of research papers have outlined the attributes and characteristics of IoT-enabled
smart cities, where IoT has applications in different sectors, ranging from agriculture,
health monitoring, transport systems, financial services, as well as energy systems [10–14].
The integration of intelligent control and communication technologies in power system
operation is a critical parameter to realise the envisioned future of IoT-enabled smart cities.
Thus, it can be predicted that the future power system will largely depend upon smart
devices and advanced technologies, leading to a smart power system network.
It goes without saying that a microgrid will need to comply with the features and
requirements of a smart energy system, as microgrids are an essential component of the
power system network. In a smart microgrid, the residential end-users will be equipped
with intelligent home energy management systems (HEMSs), which can forward the energy
generation and consumption information to a control centre or central EMS. Enabling
HEMSs with IoT technology can allow for the advanced monitoring, control and energy
management of a microgrid.
In a microgrid where users are equipped with renewable energy resources, there could
be certain time periods when some users have excess energy generated and some other
users have an energy deficit. This is not an uncommon situation since renewable energy
generation is intermittent and users’ energy demand can depend on lifestyle patterns or
weather conditions. In such cases, local (peer-to-peer) energy trading has evolved as a
natural solution to satisfy the local demand with local generation [ 15–18]. Local energy
trading applications require energy generation/consumption information to be exchanged
in real time, and hence, such applications would be much more effective when integrated
with IoT technology.
Existing research on IoT-enabled smart energy systems have focussed on energy man-
agement applications and the secure operation of the power system network. The authors
in [19] have investigated a building management system with IoT-enabled smart buildings
and discussed the key requirements for performing a number of different functions, includ-
ing demand response and building surveillance. The authors in [20] have considered the
optimum scheduling and energy efficient operation of an IoT-enabled smart city which
has the features of wireless power transfer. The authors have elaborated the requirements
of lightweight protocols, predictive models for energy forecast and context-aware energy
management for smart energy systems. IoT-enabled wind energy systems that are capable
of data acquisition, supervisory control and condition monitoring have been illustrated
in [21]. The aforementioned research papers have mainly reviewed the requirements and
expectations of the communication protocols required for an IoT-enabled microgrid.
On the other hand, the authors in [22] have utilised the fog computing platform for
energy management operations and defined the software, hardware and communication
architecture for such IoT-enabled energy management systems. A communication scheme
for blockchain-based peer-to-peer energy trading has been proposed by [ 23], where the
authors investigate metadata exchange for energy transaction blocks. For real-time opera-
tion, the authors in [24] have proposed a software infrastructure to integrate the real-time
energy profile and renewable generation data for scheduling applications in an IoT-enabled
microgrid. This can be useful for obtaining the optimum control policies for building
management. The existing research papers have mostly investigated IoT-enabled smart
energy systems at a conceptual level or from an application perspective. However, the
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 1773 3 of 22
effectiveness of IoT technology will also depend on the reliability and security features of
other aspects in the communication model, e.g., the network and physical properties.
From a communication technology perspective, different wired and wireless commu-
nication schemes have been adopted in smart grid applications. Though wired communi-
cation can offer stronger reliability and robustness, wireless communication technologies
have more flexibility and less dependence on infrastructure [ 25]. As a result, wireless
technologies are emerging as a popular solution in smart energy applications in the res-
idential context. For example, ZigBee has been deployed for appliance monitoring and
sensing applications due to its low power requirement as well as low cost. They can
allow for a transmission range of less than 100 m, which is suitable for residential energy
applications [26]. Wireless mesh networks have also been a popular choice for smart meter
deployment, where each meter has the ability to route the energy consumption data to
the nearby smart meters and form a mesh [ 27]. Though such technologies can enhance
coverage, the implementation cost and complexity can be higher. More critical energy
applications such as transmission and distribution network monitoring commonly rely
on cellular infrastructure, such as LTE, 4G and 5G networks [28,29]. Though they have a
well-developed infrastructure that can be useful in accommodating energy applications,
the infrastructure is shared with cellular applications involving voice and data usage.
Another emerging technology for smart grid communications includes WiMax, which
offers the appropriate designed security and backhaul connectivity mechanisms for critical
applications [30]. However, the technology could not progress as expected due to a more
widespread infrastructure provided by LTE and 5G networks.
Though the aforementioned technologies have been widely used for smart grid ap-
plications, they need to be adapted to meet the requirements for IoT-enabled smart grid
components. IoT applications heavily rely on low power wide area network (LPWAN)
technologies, as it allows IoT devices to operate at a lower power (thus improving the
battery life) and communicate over a wider area. It should be noted that in the context
of local energy trading, the energy supply/demand balance is achieved within nearby
households alone, which are usually within a few kilometres from each other. In this

sections.title: 2 System Model
sections.text:
We consider a smart microgrid, composed of K number of houses equipped with solar
panels, smart switches and HEMSs. The HEMSs include the functionality of scheduling
the household appliances based on renewable generation in the microgrid. Given that a
household may have excess generation or an energy deficit at certain points of time, they
can exchange the energy among each other through local energy trading. To enable energy
sharing, these HEMSs communicate with each other to identify the difference between
supply and demand in each of the houses.
The effectiveness of energy trading operations largely depends on how accurately the
generation and consumption information can be decoded by the HEMSs. The following
example will show how the errors in the communication channel can lead to a failure in
energy trading operation.
Motivating Example:
Here, we present an example of a smart microgrid with five houses equipped with
HEMSs. Let us consider that House 1 and House 2 have an excess energy of 0.3 kW and
0.7 kW, respectively, at a certain time point. On the other hand, Houses 3, 4 and 5 are
in a deficit of 0.15 kW, 0.65 kW and 0.1 kW, respectively, at the same time point. With
no errors in the communication channel in an ideal scenario, the EMS optimises energy
trading decisions as 0.15 kW power from House 1 to House 3, 0.65 kW power from House
2 to House 4 and 0.1 kW power from either House 1 or 2 to House 5. The remaining excess
energy will be sold to the power utility. Now, when the communication channel has errors,
the EMS obtains an inaccurate estimation of excess energy from Houses 1 and 2 as 0.2 kW
and 0.35 kW, respectively. On the other hand, there are also errors in the estimated demand
values for Houses 3, 4 and 5 as 0.2 kW, 0.45 kW and 0.05 kW, respectively. Now, the EMS
will make non-optimal trading decisions, delivering 0.2 kW from House 1 to House 3 and
0.35 kW from House 2 to House 4, thus leaving House 4 and House 5 in a deficit of 0.3 kW
and 0.1 kW, respectively, which the houses will need to draw from the main power grid.
However, Houses 1 and 2 had some excess energy which has to be supplied to the main
grid now. Thus, the energy trading operation is not effective.
Thus, we need to develop an efficient and reliable communication scheme, which can
manage communication channel errors more effectively, by adding multiple communication
channels. In the aforementioned microgrid, we consider that the HEMSs coordinate the
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 1773 6 of 22
energy sharing operation in a distributed manner. This is due to the fact that incorporating
a central controller will need a huge amount of information to be exchanged between the
HEMSs and the central controller. Moreover, there remains the risk of single-point failure
in such a system.
However, enabling HEMSs to directly communicate with each other will allow the
HEMSs to retrieve some information about each other without waiting for transmission
from the central controller or gateways in IoT systems. As a result, in this paper, we consider
the utilisation of overheard information from nearby HEMSs to improve information
exchange reliability. That is, the IoT-enabled HEMSs can act as communication relay nodes
that can forward overheard information to other HEMSs and can hence create multiple
communication pathways. The aforementioned system model is illustrated in Figure 1.

The new scheme enables all these HEMSs in the microgrid to communicate with each
other without involving the central controller. At the beginning, users with odd-indexed
HEMSs will transmit, whereas, the even-indexed HEMSs will act as relay nodes. Then, the
even-indexed and odd-indexed HEMSs will switch their roles between transmitters and
relays. The relay HEMSs receive the sum of signals from neighbouring HEMSs and forward
to these HEMSs so that they can cancel self-interference to extract new signals from other
HEMSs. If a HEMS receives signals from two relay HEMSs, it cancels out the common
information between these two signals and extracts the new messages. Whenever a HEMS
receives information about two different HEMSs, it computes the sum of the signals and
forwards this sum to the nearby HEMSs acting as relays. The process repeats itself as long
as all HEMSs receive each other’s information.
Let us elaborate on the above communication scheme with an example system of
five HEMSs. We denote the HEMSs as HEMS A, B, C, D and E. Let us consider that, initially,
HEMSs A, C and E transmit the energy mismatch signals and HEMSs B and D listen. HEMS
B receives the sum of signals from HEMSs A and C, whereas HEMS D receives signals from
HEMSs C and E (time slot 1). Next, HEMSs B and D transmit and HEMSs A, C and E listen
(time slot 2). HEMS A and E receive from HEMSs B and D, respectively, whereas HEMS
C receives the sum of signals from HEMSs B and D. Then, HEMS B acts as a relay and
forwards the sum of signals received in time slot 1 to A and C (time slot 3). Thus, HEMS
A and HEMS C receive the messages from each other. Then, HEMS D forwards the sum
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 1773 7 of 22
of signals to HEMSs C and E, enabling HEMSs C and E to retrieve each other’s messages
(time slot 4). Next, HEMS C forwards the sum of signals received in time slot 2 to HEMS
B and HEMS D (time slot 5). As a result, HEMSs B and D receive messages from each
other. Then, HEMS C forwards its message to HEMS B and HEMS D (time slot 6), which
allows HEMSs B and D to decode the signals from HEMS A and HEMS E, respectively.
Next HEMS B forwards the sum of HEMS C and D’s signals, whereas HEMS D forwards
the sum of HEMS B and HEMS C’s signals (time slot 7). This enables HEMS A to decode
HEMS D and HEMS E to decode HEMS B. Finally, HEMS C forwards the sum of signals
from HEMS A and E, and HEMS B and D received this sum and decode HEMS E and
HEMS A, respectively (time slot 8). Then, HEMS B (D) forwards the signal from HEMS E
(A) to HEMS A (E). (time slot 9). Thus, nine time slots are needed in this scheme for the
information exchange between five HEMSs.
Remark 1. If the IoT-enabled HEMSs communicate with each other through the control centre,
then, in the example system, HEMSs A, B, C, D and E will transmit their messages using five
different time slots in the uplink. Then, the control centre will broadcast the message of each HEMS
to all the HEMSs using five time slots in the downlink. Thus, in this scenario, a total of 10 time
slots will be needed for centralised systems, similar to the ones with the NB-IoT protocol. As a result,
the proposed scheme can significantly reduce the time delay and allow for better spectral efficiency
compared to centralised systems.
Remark 2. If the intermediate nodes decode the messages directly and forward them rather than
their sum, then, in the aforementioned example, HEMS B will directly receive the message from
HEMS A. Then, the process will continue from B to C, C to D and D to E. Thus, after four time slots,
all HEMSs will have a copy of HEMS A’s message. As a result, the information sharing among all
HEMSs will be completed in5 × 4 = 20 time slots. In effect, significant time savings can be achieved
through the proposed method compared to systems that use one-hop direct communication (such as
wireless mesh networks) where all HEMSs need to know each other’s messages for decentralised
energy management.

ual HEMSs are indexed by k. The renewable energy generation and electricity demand
managed by the kth HEMS are represented by Gk and Dk, respectively. Thus, the mismatch

After this, HEMSs A and F cancel their own signals and extract each other’s messages.

sections.title: 4 Error Probability Analysis
sections.text:
In this section, we have analytically investigated the error performance when the
kth HEMS obtains the signal from the ℓth HEMS. Similarly to the previous section, we’ll
consider the cases k odd, ℓ odd and k odd, ℓ even. The case k even, ℓ odd will have similar
expressions for error performance as the second case (k odd, ℓ even). On the other hand,
case k even, ℓ even will yield similar results to the first case (k odd, ℓ odd). This analysis
is based on binary phase shift keying (BPSK) modulation at the HEMSs, but this can
be similarly extended to quadrature phase shift keying (QPSK) modulation, since QPSK
transmissions can be considered as two orthogonal BPSK transmissions.
